title: The lowest of all
hookLine: whoever knows himself lowest of all is counted highest (Sukhmani 12)

lines: HE FALLS. ONLY AMRU, A NOBODY.
THE NOBODY BECOMES THE THIRD GURU.
cards: Sikh tradition tells of an old man who carried water. Every morning before dawn, for years, he walked to the river, filled a pitcher, and brought it back for his teacher, Guru Angad, to bathe.
One dark, stormy morning he tripped near a weaver's house and fell into the pit where the loom stood.
The weaver's wife heard the noise and said, more or less: that's only Amru, the man with no home, who wanders around after his guru. A nobody. That nobody became the third Guru, Guru Amar Das.

teach.b: Later in the twelfth ashtpadi, after the prides have been named, Guru Arjan turns the ladder over. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa.
Whoever knows himself to be low is counted the highest of all. Neechaa: low, beneath. Oochaa: high, above.
Ordinary Punjabi, words for a shelf or a hill. The verb in the middle matters: ganeeai, is counted, is reckoned. The line doesn't say the humble person feels high, or gets promoted at work.
It says that in the real reckoning, God's count, the order is reversed.

teach.h: THE DUST OF ALL SEES EVERY HEART.
teach.b: The next line deepens it: the one whose mind becomes the dust of all recognizes the Name in every heart. That's why the low place works: when you're not looking down on anyone, you can finally see what's in them.
Tradition says when Guru Angad heard what the weaver's wife had called Amar Das, the homeless one, he called him the home of the homeless. The insult became a title.

Tradition says Amar Das was already an old man when he became Guru, and asked everyone who came to see him, even, in the story, the emperor Akbar, to eat first in the langar, in the same rows as everyone else.
The lowest seat, made into the door. So this isn't a trick for getting ahead. The stanza describes how things are already counted.
We just can't see the scoreboard.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water for Guru Angad as a model of seva, and in gurdwaras today volunteers wash dishes, sweep and mind shoes, often without anyone knowing their names.

o: far away, out of reach of others
low, beneath, the place of the humble
hidden, kept quietly out of sight

games.q: the lowest of all — tap the pairs.
p: the water carrier, later third Guru

s: the line promises humble people success at work
ganeeai means counted: the reversal is in God's reckoning, not a promotion.
Guru Amar Das was elderly when he became Guru
tradition remembers him as an old man by then.
the weaver's wife praised Amar Das as a great man
she called him a homeless nobody; tradition says Guru Angad turned it into a title.

games.q: you're Guru Angad. someone has mocked your devoted student as a homeless nobody. what do you say?
o: call him the home of the homeless.
games.why: tradition says he called Amar Das the home of the homeless: the insult became a title.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose day you could make easier, a roommate, a coworker, someone at home, and one small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: the dishes, a refilled water jug, a door held.
Picture yourself doing it and walking away without a word, and let that feel like enough.

wordCard.voice: Neechaa, low, beneath. Whoever knows himself neechaa is counted highest, the way an old water carrier became the third Guru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: neechaa, low; paired in the line with oochaa, high.

carryVoice: Your line: lowest is highest. The homeless one became the home of the homeless. More tomorrow.
